source: Kittaka, Mikami, Shimada (2021) Passive or Active? Behavioral changes in different designs of search experiments
finding: Same search model, three experiment designs (passive cutoff, quasi-active one offer at a time, active choose among options). Subjects under-searched in all three. Passive design gave the most under-search.
numbers: 103 students, within-subject, 20 spells per design. Mean searches: passive 3.095, quasi-active 3.133, active 3.380; risk-neutral optimum 4.537. Payoff 8.298/8.437/8.413 vs 9.028 optimal; payoff gaps not significant. Active gave more searches than the others (1% aggregate, 5% individual).
limits: Single online lab study in Japan, students. Table layout in the PDF text was garbled; column order read as passive, quasi-active, active.
agent_relevance: How the agent is asked to stop (commit to a threshold vs decide each step) changes how long it searches. Prompt design is a moderator, not noise.

source: Kittaka, Mikami, Shimada (2021) Passive or Active? Behavioral changes in different designs of search experiments
finding: Most subjects used a constant reservation value within a design (one-step-forward rule). Recall of earlier offers was rare and about equal across designs.
numbers: Recall prevalence about 12% in all designs (11.2-12.8%). Termination rate about 30% per search (passive 31.6%, quasi 29.9%, active 28.4%). In the passive design: 31.6% of spells one choice, 31.6% same cutoff, 28.7% decreasing, 7.9% increasing; decreasing-cutoff spells had a higher average cutoff (9.87 vs 8.91).
limits: Decreasing cutoffs also seen by Brown, Flinn and Schotter (2011) per this paper; not checked.
agent_relevance: A fixed-threshold stop rule is a reasonable model and default for the agent.

source: Kittaka, Mikami, Shimada (2021) Passive or Active? Behavioral changes in different designs of search experiments
finding: Risk preference (Holt-Laury list) predicted search length only in the passive design. Prior studies disagree on whether risk or loss aversion drives under-search.
numbers: Risk effect significant only in passive design. Cited: Schunk (2009) loss aversion not risk preference; Miura et al. (2017) and Bhatia et al. (2021) the opposite. Nachman (1972) theory: more risk-averse means lower reservation value.
limits: Mixed prior evidence, design-dependent.
agent_relevance: Under-search is not settled as risk aversion. Do not build a risk-aversion fix into the stop rule.

source: Marcu and Noussair (2022) Sequential Search with a Price Freeze Option: Theory and Experimental Evidence
finding: Lab test of search with a price-freeze option (a paid right to recall an offer). Treatment effects matched model predictions. A modest but significant tendency to stop too early remained in most treatments.
numbers: 177 undergraduates at Arizona; 180 search problems per subject counted toward pay. Manipulated freeze cost, time horizon, recall (none or imperfect).
limits: Student sample; seller side exogenous.
agent_relevance: Cheap options to keep a candidate while continuing (like keeping a draft) are used as theory predicts.

source: Marcu and Noussair (2022) Sequential Search with a Price Freeze Option: Theory and Experimental Evidence
finding: Lower freeze fee increased under-searching. Early stopping cost little profit.
numbers: Authors report profit losses from under-searching are small; lowering the fee magnifies exploration below optimum.
limits: Short-run, one-sided model; no seller response.
agent_relevance: Under-search is often cheap. Over-search (wasted compute) may be the bigger cost for an LLM.

source: Marcu and Noussair (2022) Sequential Search with a Price Freeze Option: Theory and Experimental Evidence
finding: Rival explanations for early stopping did not beat the plain optimal-search model: regret, sunk-cost inclusion, misperceived horizon, risk aversion.
numbers: Paper says none of the four improves on the baseline. Cites Cox and Oaxaca (1989) for risk aversion, Sonnemans (1998) that only a small share of early stops fit reasonable risk aversion, Kogut (1990) sunk costs, Gabaix et al. (2006) cognitive costs.
limits: Negative result in one design; cited studies not opened.
agent_relevance: No single behavioural fix explains under-search, so a generic 'search a bit more' correction is a guess.

source: Marcu and Noussair (2022) Sequential Search with a Price Freeze Option: Theory and Experimental Evidence
finding: Literature summary: early stopping relative to the reservation rule is the typical finding across decades of search experiments.
numbers: Cited: Kahan et al. (1967) groups searched longer than individuals; Rapoport and Tversky (1970) near optimal with some early stopping; Schotter and Braunstein (1981); Cox and Oaxaca (1989); Sonnemans (1998); Kogut (1990); Einav (2005).
limits: Secondhand for the cited primaries.
agent_relevance: Base rate: humans stop early. LLMs trained on human text may copy it (untested here).

source: Brown, Flinn, Schotter (2011) Real-time search in the laboratory and the market
finding: Lab search with cutoffs chosen each period; cited as showing declining reservation values over time.
numbers: Not opened; known only from description in Kittaka et al. (2021).
limits: Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Declining thresholds resemble an agent lowering its bar as budget runs down.

source: Schotter and Braunstein (1981) Economic search: an experimental study
finding: Early lab test of search theory: tests recall, induced risk aversion, offer distribution, information.
numbers: Not opened; described in Marcu and Noussair (2022).
limits: Secondhand only.
agent_relevance: Founding experimental design for the stop rule.

source: Cox and Oaxaca (1989) Laboratory experiments with a finite-horizon job-search model
finding: Subjects stopped earlier than optimal; the authors attributed this to risk aversion.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Secondhand; challenged by Sonnemans (1998) per Marcu and Noussair.
agent_relevance: Rival-explanation example.

source: Goldstein, McAfee, Suri, Wright (2020) Learning When to Stop Searching (repeated secretary problem), Management Science
finding: When people play a secretary-type game repeatedly with a learnable value distribution, they learn near-optimal stopping quickly. Earlier work with one-shot or hidden-distribution games found little learning.
numbers: 6,537 players, 48,336 games. Optimal win rate with known distribution: 62.2% (7 boxes) and just under 60% (15 boxes); classic no-information rate about 41% (7) and 39% (15), converging to 1/e. Human win rates came within 5 to 10 points of the maximum after a few games; an idealized learner reaches the maximum in 7 or fewer games.
limits: Online, self-selected players, values shown not ranks; blinded Management Science manuscript.
agent_relevance: Strong moderator: feedback over repeated trials. An agent with memory of past search outcomes can calibrate thresholds; a single-shot agent cannot.

source: Goldstein, McAfee, Suri, Wright (2020) Learning When to Stop Searching (repeated secretary problem), Management Science
finding: First-game errors go in both directions. Learning was steep over the first games and recovered even after unhelpful first-game feedback.
numbers: First game: stopped about 25% of the time below the critical value (too early) and at most 75% above it (too late) instead of 100%. Games 2-4 close to the ideal 50% at the critical value. Restricting to players with many games gave the same trend.
limits: Fitted threshold models best described players; not a causal intervention.
agent_relevance: Calibrating stops needs a few instances of feedback; first attempts are noisy both ways.

source: Spiliopoulos, Rapoport, Seale (2023) Progressive stopping heuristics that excel in individual and competitive sequential search, Theory and Decision
finding: Simple descriptive heuristics do well only when the optimal secretary rule has one threshold. A progressive-stopping heuristic (ratio of interviewed to remaining) does well when the optimal rule has many thresholds that relax over time.
numbers: Progressive stopping reaches more than 95% of optimal performance across three multi-threshold variants and many sequence lengths; a related rule reaches 98.5% of the optimum for n up to 100,000 in expected-rank minimisation (Krieger and Samuel-Cahn 2009).
limits: Simulation of ideal heuristic performance, not human data. Rank-only problems.
agent_relevance: A stop rule whose bar loosens as the budget runs out is near-optimal and trivial to implement.

source: Spiliopoulos, Rapoport, Seale (2023) Progressive stopping heuristics that excel in individual and competitive sequential search, Theory and Decision
finding: Competitive variant with several employers hiring at once: authors give a subgame-perfect equilibrium and an inverse progressive-stopping heuristic with near-optimal performance.
numbers: Corrects the proof of Karlin and Lei (2015). Heuristic performs very well for the whole set of employers per authors.
limits: Theory and simulation only.
agent_relevance: Contention for the same candidates changes the stop rule; relevant only if agents share a pool.

source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) The Art of Knowing When to Stop: Optimal Stopping in People and Machines (NeurIPS 2024 workshop)
finding: Human data on a finite-horizon stopping task (combinatorial innovation, switch from extract to fuse). People mostly switched once. They stopped too early in three conditions and too late in one.
numbers: 210 participants, four conditions (p in {0.8,0.2}, w in {3,1.5}), 7 official tasks of 10 steps. Optimal switch at step 9 (high p, high w): only 32% switched there. Optimal step 0 (low p, low w): only 18% did.
limits: Reanalysis of an earlier behavioural experiment (Zhao and Griffiths 2024); small design.
agent_relevance: Direction of error depends on payoff structure, not a single bias to under-search.

source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) The Art of Knowing When to Stop: Optimal Stopping in People and Machines (NeurIPS 2024 workshop)
finding: LLMs as simulated participants. GPT-4 and Llama-3.1 mostly switched once but at the wrong place; GPT-3.5 often switched repeatedly.
numbers: Switch-once share for GPT-3.5: 71.4% (HH), 14.3% (HL), 57.1% (LH), 28.6% (LL) vs about 80% for people. HH: GPT-4 and Llama most common switch at step 5, 4 steps early (optimum 9). LL (optimum step 0): GPT-4 switched at step 5, Llama-3.1 at step 3, over-exploring.
limits: Few LLM runs; preliminary workshop paper.
agent_relevance: LLMs misplace stops in both directions, worse than people in extreme conditions. Do not trust the model's own stop.

source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) The Art of Knowing When to Stop: Optimal Stopping in People and Machines (NeurIPS 2024 workshop)
finding: Giving LLMs the MDP solution or chain-of-thought did not reliably fix stopping; the paper says CoT may help partly.
numbers: Compared Direct Play, MDP prompt and COT prompt for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. Authors say mathematical solutions alone were insufficient to find the optimal switch point.
limits: Preliminary; no significance tests seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Handing the agent a formula does not make it stop correctly. An external stop controller is safer.

source: Kalayci, Raman, Dughmi (2025) Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
finding: Treats each LLM generation as opening a Pandora's box. A UCB-style Weitzman algorithm decides when to stop sampling without knowing the reward distribution.
numbers: Same quality as non-adaptive Best-of-N with 15-35% fewer generations at acceptance rates 0.75 and above, savings rising from 15% to 35% as targets tighten. Win rate over equal-budget Best-of-N above 54% across most costs c in [1e-5, 1e-3]. 1,600 generation profiles; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 with RM-Mistral-7B; AlpacaFarm and HH-RLHF.
limits: Gains rest on the reward model being a good proxy; upper-confidence estimate needed to avoid stopping too early. Win-rate gain modest.
agent_relevance: Direct use of Weitzman values to decide when more samples are worth their cost. Matches our S0 gate idea.

source: Pilditch (2026) Knowing When to Stop: Bayesian Optimal Stopping for LLM Evaluations (optstop)
finding: Precision-based adaptive stopping for LLM evaluation runs. Samples where uncertainty is high, stops where estimates are stable.
numbers: Nine validation cells, 200 items (198 for GPQA Diamond), 10 epochs per item, precision 0.05, 97% credible intervals. Efficiency gains 57.2% to 97.3%, mean 81.1%; continuous mean 95.1%, ordinal 75.0%, binary 73.3%. Mean absolute score deviation 0.006 on 0-1 scale.
limits: Stops measurement, not reasoning. Savings depend on evaluation design; safeguard needed near zero performance.
agent_relevance: Useful for our own benchmark runs; saves repeated runs at fixed precision.

source: Wikipedia: Search theory
finding: Textbook statement of the three main models: Stigler fixed-sample price search, McCall reservation wage, Weitzman Pandora's box.
numbers: Pandora's rule: open boxes in decreasing order of reservation value; stop when best payoff exceeds the remaining reservation values (Weitzman 1979). Olszewski and Weber (2015) extend it to broader payoffs. Higher offer variance can raise the reservation wage (McCall 1970).
limits: Encyclopedia; no experimental numbers; no Koopman content.
agent_relevance: Pandora's rule is the one-line stop/continue policy for costly independent options.

source: Wikipedia: Bayesian search theory
finding: Koopman's Search and Screening (1946, OEG Report 56) is the founding text; Bayesian search was used for Thresher (1964) and Scorpion (1968) and cited for Air France 447.
numbers: After a failed search of a cell: p' = p(1-q)/(1-pq). Scorpion lay about 740 km SW of the Azores under over 3,000 m; the initial East Coast search found nothing.
limits: Page flagged as needing citations; Koopman's content not described; no count of failed hunts.
agent_relevance: A failed search lowers but does not zero a region's probability: 'nothing found' is evidence. The agent can apply this to dead ends.

source: Caplin and Dean (2010) Enhanced Choice Experiments
finding: Proposes choice-process experiments that record search order so reservation levels can be extracted. Search with satisficing stops once a reservation utility is found.
numbers: Methods draft; no effect sizes read. Search-result snippet says the 2011 Caplin, Dean, Martin paper found reservation utilities respond systematically to the environment.
limits: Methods draft only; the 2011 paper's numbers were not read.
agent_relevance: The reservation level depends on context; the agent's bar should adapt.

source: Rapoport and Tversky (1970) Choice behavior in an optional stopping task
finding: Subjects near optimal with some early stopping; seven subjects saw 15,600 draws over weeks before playing.
numbers: Not opened; described in two opened papers.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Long exposure to the distribution produces near-optimal stops, consistent with the learning result.

source: Kahan, Rapoport, Jones (1967) Decision making in a sequential search task
finding: Offer distribution had little effect on decision quality; groups searched longer than individuals.
numbers: Groups of 22 participants, up to 200 draws; not opened.
limits: Secondhand; old design.
agent_relevance: Group deliberation may lengthen search, a hint for multi-agent ensembles.

source: Weitzman (1979) Optimal Search for the Best Alternative, Econometrica 47(3):641-654
finding: Index rule: each alternative has a reservation value; open in decreasing order; stop when the best found exceeds all remaining indices.
numbers: Not opened; rule as described in Wikipedia and Kalayci et al.
limits: Needs independent boxes with known distributions and costs; weak with correlated options.
agent_relevance: Basis for any cost-aware stop rule.
